source_refs.note: Exercise 1.3, Question 1 (book p. 23-24); answers book p. 298-299 (PDF 300-301)

blocks.prompt: 1 (i) Let \(f(x) = \log_{4}(x - 2)\). Show that \(f(x)\) is a one-to-one function using the horizontal line test.
blocks.explanation:
A graph question: is f one-to-one? We must show it with the horizontal line test.
Given \(f(x) = \log_{4}(x - 2)\). Plan: find the domain, sketch the graph from a table, then show that any line \(y = c\) meets the graph only once.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = \log_{4}(x - 2)\).
To prove: f is one-to-one, using the horizontal line test.
Method: a function is one-to-one if every horizontal line meets its graph at most once. We draw the graph, then solve f(x) = c for a general c to show there is only one x.

Find the domain
\[x - 2 > 0\]
\[x > 2\]
Why: a logarithm is defined only for positive numbers.

Make a table of values
\[x = 2.25:\ \log_{4}\tfrac{1}{4} = -1\]
\[x = 3:\ \log_{4}1 = 0\]
\[x = 6:\ \log_{4}4 = 1\]
\[x = 18:\ \log_{4}16 = 2\]
Why: we choose \(x\) so that \(x - 2\) is a power of 4; then the logarithm is a whole number.

Shape of the graph
\(f(x) = \log_{4}(x - 2)\) is \(y = \log_{4}x\) shifted 2 units to the right, so its vertical asymptote is \(x = 2\) and it cuts the \(x\)-axis at \((3, 0)\). The base \(4 > 1\), so the graph is strictly increasing.
Why: it has the form \(f(x - h)\) with \(h = 2\) (Section 1.9).

Horizontal line test with \(y = c\)
\[\log_{4}(x - 2) = c\]
\[x - 2 = 4^{c}\]
\[x = 4^{c} + 2\]
Why: \(\log_{a}u = c\) means \(u = a^{c}\). For each value of \(c\) there is exactly one \(x\), and it is greater than 2 (because \(4^{c} > 0\)), so it lies in the domain.

Check:
The line \(y = 1\) meets the graph only at \((6, 1)\) and the line \(y = 2\) only at \((18, 2)\); in the figure each dashed line cuts the curve once.
blocks.final_answer: Every horizontal line \(y = c\) meets the graph of \(f\) exactly once (at \(x = 4^{c} + 2\)). Hence proved: \(f(x) = \log_{4}(x - 2)\) is one-to-one.

answer_figure.alt: Graph of y = log base 4 of (x - 2) rising from the dashed asymptote x = 2 through (2.25, -1), (3, 0), (6, 1) and (18, 2); the dashed horizontal lines y = -1, y = 1 and y = 2 each cut the curve exactly once.
answer_figure.caption: f(x) = log₄(x − 2) with horizontal lines: each meets the curve once

blocks.prompt: 1 (ii) Let \(f(x) = \log_{4}(x - 2)\). Find the inverse function \(f^{-1}(x)\) algebraically.
blocks.explanation:
Find an inverse by algebra.
Given \(y = \log_{4}(x - 2)\). Plan: change the log form into exponential form, make \(x\) the subject, then interchange \(x\) and \(y\).
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = \log_{4}(x - 2)\), one-to-one (part (i)).
To find: \(f^{-1}(x)\).
Method: put \(y = f(x)\), solve for \(x\) in terms of \(y\), then interchange \(x\) and \(y\).

Write \(y = f(x)\)
\[y = \log_{4}(x - 2)\]
Why: the inverse undoes this rule, so we start from it.

Change to exponential form
\[4^{y} = x - 2\]
Why: \(\log_{a}u = y\) is the same statement as \(a^{y} = u\).

Make \(x\) the subject
\[x = 4^{y} + 2\]
Why: add 2 to both sides.

Interchange \(x\) and \(y\)
\[y = 4^{x} + 2\]
\[f^{-1}(x) = 4^{x} + 2\]
Why: the inverse takes the outputs of f as its inputs, so x and y swap roles.

Check:
\[f(f^{-1}(x)) = \log_{4}(4^{x} + 2 - 2)\]
\[= \log_{4}4^{x} = x\]
Composing f with the answer gives x back.

blocks.prompt: 1 (iii) Let \(f(x) = \log_{4}(x - 2)\). State the domain and range of \(f(x)\) and \(f^{-1}(x)\).
blocks.explanation:
State domains and ranges.
Given \(f(x) = \log_{4}(x - 2)\) and \(f^{-1}(x) = 4^{x} + 2\). Plan: find the domain and range of \(f\), then swap them for \(f^{-1}\) and confirm from its formula.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = \log_{4}(x - 2)\), \(f^{-1}(x) = 4^{x} + 2\).
To find: \(D_{f}, R_{f}, D_{f^{-1}}, R_{f^{-1}}\).
Method: the inverse swaps inputs and outputs, so the domain of one is the range of the other.

Domain of \(f\)
\[x - 2 > 0 \Rightarrow x > 2\]
\[D_{f} = \,]2, \infty[\]
Why: a logarithm needs a positive argument.

Range of \(f\)
\[R_{f} = \,]-\infty, \infty[\]
Why: as \(x\) runs over \(]2, \infty[\), \(x - 2\) takes every positive value, and a logarithm takes every real value on the positive numbers (part (i): every \(y = c\) is reached).

Domain and range of \(f^{-1}\)
\[D_{f^{-1}} = R_{f} = \,]-\infty, \infty[\]
\[R_{f^{-1}} = D_{f} = \,]2, \infty[\]
Why: inputs and outputs are interchanged.

Check:
\(4^{x}\) is defined for every real \(x\), and \(4^{x} > 0\), so \(4^{x} + 2 > 2\) and it takes every value above 2. This agrees with \(D_{f^{-1}}\) and \(R_{f^{-1}}\).

blocks.prompt: 1 (iv) Let \(f(x) = \log_{4}(x - 2)\). Verify graphically that the graphs of \(f(x)\) and \(f^{-1}(x)\) are symmetric about the line \(y = x\).
blocks.explanation:
Draw both graphs and the line y = x on one plane.
Given \(f(x) = \log_{4}(x - 2)\) and \(f^{-1}(x) = 4^{x} + 2\). Plan: plot points of \(f\), swap their coordinates to get points of \(f^{-1}\), and show each pair is a mirror image in \(y = x\).
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = \log_{4}(x - 2)\), \(f^{-1}(x) = 4^{x} + 2\).
To verify: the two graphs are symmetric about \(y = x\).
Method: \((a, b)\) is on \(f\) exactly when \((b, a)\) is on \(f^{-1}\); the point \((b, a)\) is the reflection of \((a, b)\) in \(y = x\).

Points of f and of the inverse
\[(2.25, -1) \leftrightarrow (-1, 2.25)\]
\[(3, 0) \leftrightarrow (0, 3)\]
\[(6, 1) \leftrightarrow (1, 6)\]
Check one: \(4^{1} + 2 = 6\), so \((1, 6)\) is on \(f^{-1}\).
Why: each point of the inverse is a point of f with its coordinates interchanged.

Why \((b, a)\) is the mirror image of \((a, b)\)
\[\text{slope} = \dfrac{a - b}{b - a} = -1\]
\[\text{midpoint} = \left(\tfrac{a+b}{2}, \tfrac{a+b}{2}\right)\]
Why: the joining segment is perpendicular to \(y = x\) (slope \(-1\) against slope 1) and its midpoint lies on \(y = x\). So \(y = x\) is the perpendicular bisector: a mirror.

Asymptotes and intercepts also reflect
The vertical asymptote \(x = 2\) of \(f\) becomes the horizontal asymptote \(y = 2\) of \(f^{-1}\); the \(x\)-intercept \((3, 0)\) becomes the \(y\)-intercept \((0, 3)\).
Why: these are made of points, and every point reflects.

Check:
In the figure the dashed segments are cut in half by y = x at right angles; folding the page along y = x puts one curve exactly on the other.
blocks.final_answer: The graph of \(f^{-1}(x) = 4^{x} + 2\) is the reflection of the graph of \(f(x) = \log_{4}(x - 2)\) in the line \(y = x\), so the two graphs are symmetric about \(y = x\).

answer_figure.alt: The curve f(x) = log base 4 of (x - 2) with asymptote x = 2, the curve f inverse (x) = 4 to the power x plus 2 with asymptote y = 2, and the line y = x. Dashed segments join (3, 0) to (0, 3), (6, 1) to (1, 6) and (2.25, -1) to (-1, 2.25), each cut in half by y = x.
answer_figure.caption: f and f⁻¹ are mirror images in the line y = x

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key prints the label (iii) twice for Question 1. The second (iii), with the graphs of \(f(x) = \log_{4}(x - 2)\) and \(f^{-1}(x) = 4^{x} + 2\), is the answer to part (iv).
